questions.q: Per this lesson, why does a flat, unconnected list of terms stop working as a glossary grows?
options: It makes browsing nearly impossible, so someone can't discover closely related terms
Flat lists are technically impossible to store in any database
Flat lists always contain duplicate entries
Alphabetical ordering is illegal in most jurisdictions
questions.explain: Without structure, someone searching for 'Revenue' has no way to discover that 'Net Revenue' and 'Gross Revenue' are closely related, more specific concepts.

questions.q: In this lesson's worked example, what is the relationship between 'Revenue' and 'Net Revenue'?
options: Hierarchy — Revenue is broader, Net Revenue is narrower
Synonym — they mean exactly the same thing
No relationship at all
They are competing, contradictory definitions
questions.explain: Revenue is the broader parent concept; Net Revenue is a more specific, narrower child term underneath it in the hierarchy.

questions.q: What should happen when a glossary identifies two terms that mean exactly the same thing, per this lesson?
options: One should be marked the official term, with the other marked as a synonym pointing to it
Both should be kept as separate, competing official entries
The less popular term should be deleted with no trace
They should be merged into a single hierarchy with no synonym relationship recorded
questions.explain: A good glossary picks one official term and marks the other as a synonym pointing to it, rather than maintaining two separate competing entries for the same concept.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say treating 'Customer' and 'Account' as true synonyms would be a modeling mistake?
options: Because a single customer might have multiple accounts, so they aren't actually identical concepts
Because the words have different numbers of letters
Because synonyms are never allowed in any glossary
Because 'Account' is always a more official term than 'Customer'
questions.explain: They are near-synonyms, not true synonyms — collapsing them would silently lose a real distinction (one customer, multiple accounts) the business actually relies on; 'related term' is the honest relationship.

questions.q: Per this lesson, does a child term in a hierarchy (like 'Net Revenue, North America') need its own definition?
options: Yes — it should still pass the four-part test on its own, not leave its specifics implicit
No — child terms automatically inherit their parent's exact definition with no changes
No — only the top-level parent term in a hierarchy needs a definition
Only if the child term has fewer than two words in its name
questions.explain: Each child term needs its own specific, measurable, self-contained, implementation-free definition (from Lesson 7's test) — not just an implied variation on the parent's definition.
